Haypp: the right kind of business at the wrong point in its expectations cycle

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The conclusion for your decisionHaypp's fundamentals over the next three years are skewed to the positive, but the direction of estimate revisions over the next six to twelve months is skewed to the negative. At SEK 154.80 the shares already pay for the brokers' faster recovery, so our forecast returns only about +1% to March 2028 at the fair multiple. The unusually positive skew you look for is not here yet. It can arrive by one of two dated routes (a reset of estimates followed by delivery, or a supplier-contract surprise in May 2027), or through a lower entry price: at SEK 116, the same forecast and multiple return about +35% to March 2028.

What Haypp is. Haypp is a retail-media business wrapped inside a thin-margin online shop. The shop sells nicotine pouches at a product gross margin of under 9%. More than half of Haypp's gross profit comes from Media and Insights: advertising, launch services and consumer data sold to the same manufacturers that supply the pouches. This memo calls that income "supplier-paid income". Supplier-paid income explains Haypp's moat, its main risk and most of its earnings sensitivity. The opportunity is the sales channel itself: online is only about 3% of pouch sales in the United States.

The business is better than its earnings, and the shares are ahead of both. Three things are true at once:

  1. The fundamental case over three to four years is strong and mostly mechanical. Heavy users of nicotine pouches move online as their daily use rises. Haypp holds most of the online channel in every market it serves. The mature Nordic segment (Core) already earns a 12.5% EBITDA margin and funds the expansion. The infrastructure for a business twice Haypp's size is built and paid for. Our forecast has revenue compounding at about 16% a year to 2030, and EPS rising from SEK 2.27 (2026) to SEK 7.17 (2028) and SEK 13.34 (2030).
  2. The brokers' expectations already sit above our forecast. Our 2027 and 2028 EPS are 27% and 24% below the brokers' median, and our revenue is 5% and 8% below it. Our 2028 revenue is also about 9% below the floor of the company's own target. The median broker has not cut its 2027 estimates; it has moved the recovery into 2027.
  3. The share price pays for the brokers' version. The shares trade on 23.9 times our two-year-forward EPS, against a guideline fair multiple of 14.45 times. Over the next 18 months, 67% growth in forward earnings is almost exactly cancelled by the fall in the multiple. At the guideline multiple, the model's total return is +1% to March 2028 and +36% (11% a year) to September 2029.

The skew is the point of this memo. Haypp's fundamental outcomes over three years are skewed to the positive. The probability of guidance and sell-side upgrades over the next six to twelve months is skewed to the negative. The next two reports (10 February and early May 2027) can damage the thesis but cannot confirm it, because Haypp's margin comparison against a year earlier is flat or down by construction in both quarters. The first report that can confirm the thesis is the second-quarter report in mid-August 2027.

What would turn Haypp into one of your situations. Two routes would give the case positive skew in both fundamentals and upgrades, and both can be tracked on dated reports. Route (a) is delivery after a reset: the brokers cut 2027 to about our level, and Haypp then delivers the margin step. Expectations would sit at or below delivery, and the first estimate upgrades in two years would become possible. Route (b) is a positive surprise from the 2027 supplier contracts, the first priced on a Growth customer base about 55% larger than a year earlier. If those contracts re-price accordingly, our forecast moves up instead of the brokers' coming down. The earlier Analyst gives this upper case a probability of about 18%. I agree that the 2027 supplier contracts are the one live source of positive surprise inside six months.

Why the risk is manageable to analyse. The case is simple in structure and fragile in numbers. Three quantities decide it, and Haypp publishes all three every quarter. The fragility comes from a 2.3% operating margin, from three suppliers that hold about 87% of pouch volume, and from a multiple with no peer anchor beneath it.

The five judgements that move the value most, with the arithmetic

One conversion is used throughout: in 2027, SEK 10m of EBITDA equals SEK 0.24 of EPS (SEK 10m, less 25% tax, divided by about 31.4m shares). Our 2027 base case is EBITDA of SEK 309m and EPS of SEK 4.26; our 2028 base case is EBITDA of SEK 431m and EPS of SEK 7.17.

Judgement 1: how fast the Growth segment (United States and United Kingdom) grows. Growth revenue matters little for 2027 EPS and a great deal for 2028 to 2030, the years on which the share price rests. We assume Growth revenue of SEK 2,010m in 2027 and SEK 2,613m in 2028; the brokers' geographic split implies growth of +48% and +37.5%.

  • Step 1: ten points of extra growth in 2027 is 10% of 2026 Growth revenue of SEK 1,498m, or SEK 150m.
  • Step 2: the value of that revenue depends on whether supplier income follows in the same year. Product revenue alone leaves about 6.5 öre of contribution per krona (a product gross margin of about 8.7%, less fulfilment), which is SEK 10m. With supplier income following, contribution is about 15%, which is SEK 22m.
  • Step 3: SEK 10m to 22m of EBITDA is SEK 0.24 to 0.54 of EPS, or 6% to 13% of SEK 4.26.
  • Step 4: the error compounds, and by 2028 supplier income has caught up through the annual contracts. Ten points more growth in both years gives Growth revenue of SEK 1,498m x 1.44 x 1.40 = SEK 3,020m, which is SEK 407m above our forecast. At a 15% contribution, the extra revenue adds SEK 61m of EBITDA and SEK 1.49 of EPS, 21% of SEK 7.17. Ten points less growth in both years gives SEK 2,229m of revenue, SEK 58m less EBITDA and SEK 1.41 less EPS.

Judgement 2: whether management holds costs while the growth window is open. The forecast depends on cost restraint more than on any other judgement, and the market discusses it least. A slip in cost restraint would still fall far short of a repeat of 2026, but it would be enough to put 2027 EPS at or below Pareto's SEK 3.58.

  • Step 1: the forecast needs the costs between gross profit and EBITDA to rise by only SEK 78m in 2027, from SEK 701m to SEK 779m.
  • Step 2: if overheads grow 15% instead of about 9%, costs rise by a further SEK 30m. If marketing runs at 2.8% of sales instead of 2.2%, the extra 0.6% of SEK 5,524m of revenue adds SEK 33m.
  • Step 3: either slip alone takes 2027 EBITDA to about SEK 278m and cuts EPS by SEK 0.72 to 0.79 (17% to 19%). Both slips together take EBITDA to SEK 246m and EPS to SEK 2.75, a fall of 35%.
  • Step 4: the favourable case is smaller. Marketing at 1.7% of sales would add SEK 28m of EBITDA and SEK 0.66 of EPS (15%).

Judgement 3: how fast supplier-paid income grows, and whether the 2027 contracts re-price the United States customer base. Supplier-paid income is the most powerful line in the forecast, and our inputs hold a cushion against it.

  • Step 1: supplier-paid income is about SEK 570m in 2026 and carries almost no direct cost. Ten points of growth in supplier-paid income is therefore SEK 57m of gross profit.
  • Step 2: SEK 57m of gross profit is SEK 1.36 of EPS, 32% of SEK 4.26, if nothing offsets it.
  • Step 3: the forecast inputs hold a cushion. The earlier Analyst describes 30% growth in supplier-paid income, but our gross-margin input needs only about 20% growth if the product margin merely holds at its current level. Growth of 20% therefore leaves the forecast intact. Growth of 10% costs SEK 57m, unless management gives less away in consumer prices; giving less away is management's habit, and it moves the damage from profit to revenue growth.
  • Step 4: the upside. Supplier income earned in Growth is about 11% of Growth revenue, down from about 13% a year earlier (derived). A return to 13% on SEK 2,010m of revenue would add SEK 40m to 45m of EBITDA, about SEK 1.0 of EPS, or 23% to 25%.

Judgement 4: whether a supplier or a regulator interrupts Haypp's right to sell. The precedent is Philip Morris pausing online sales of ZYN in the United States in 2024, when ZYN was 46% of Haypp's United States sales.

  • Step 1: Growth revenue 25% below our forecast for a year is SEK 500m of lost revenue.
  • Step 2: at Growth's gross margin of about 19%, less 3% of fulfilment cost saved, the lost revenue costs SEK 80m of EBITDA. If the supplier in dispute also trims its Nordic media spending, the loss rises by SEK 30m to 50m. The total of SEK 110m to 130m is SEK 2.6 to 3.1 of EPS, leaving 2027 EPS of SEK 1.2 to 1.6.
  • Step 3: management would respond. Cutting marketing to 1% of sales saves about SEK 70m a year, about half of it in the first year, which leaves 2027 EPS at about SEK 2.0 to 2.5.
  • Step 4: at a 12% probability, the expected cost to 2027 EPS is about SEK 0.25 (6%). The damage to the share price would be far larger than the damage to earnings, because the multiple would fall towards its trough at the same time (topic 9).
  • Where I differ from the earlier Analyst: the earlier Analyst puts the severe case at EPS of SEK 1.0 to 1.5; my arithmetic gives that figure only before management responds.

Judgement 5: the multiple investors pay in spring 2028 for the earnings of 2029 and 2030. The 18-month return is the small difference between two large numbers. It is set by what investors in spring 2028 believe about 2029 and 2030, the two years in which Growth is forecast to move into profit.

  • Step 1: the model's value at the 18-month column is the guideline multiple times the two-year-forward EPS at that date: 14.45 x SEK 10.83 = SEK 156.5.
  • Step 2: SEK 10.83 is, in substance, EPS for the year to March 2030: three-quarters of 2029 (SEK 10.08) and one-quarter of 2030 (SEK 13.34).
  • Step 3: one turn of the multiple is worth SEK 10.8 per share, or 7% of today's price. The chart below shows the value at five multiples, from SEK 127 (-18%) at 11.7 times to SEK 199 (+29%) at 18.4 times, which is today's multiple on the brokers' estimates.
  • Step 4: EPS 10% lower than SEK 10.83 at the guideline multiple gives SEK 141 (-9%).

Taken together, the 2027 EPS distribution is skewed down: about SEK 5.6 in the upper case (18% probability), SEK 4.26 in the base case (50%), SEK 2.3 in the lower case (20%) and about SEK 2.0 after a severe event (12%). The probability-weighted figure is about SEK 3.8, roughly 10% below our base case and a third below the brokers' median of SEK 5.80.

Scorecard

1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Bottom line: the external tailwinds for revenue are strong, structural and multi-year, but the profit they support is granted by three suppliers and a handful of regulators, so Haypp lacks only gradual headwinds, not sudden ones.

Evidence: the dominant external force is a change of channel, not of category. Online is about 36% of pouch sales in Sweden, about 7% in the United Kingdom and about 3% in the United States. Users move online once they use seven to eight pouches a day, because at that level the online saving (40% to 50% against a United States store) outweighs the wait for delivery. The average American user consumes 3.6 to 4 pouches a day, and Philip Morris's own research shows daily use rising from 5.2 pouches in a user's first year to 7.4 after three years. Each cohort of American users therefore drifts over the online threshold with time.

Four further tailwinds sit on top of channel migration:

  • The global pouch category is forecast to grow about 21% a year in value to 2029.
  • State taxes raise shelf prices and push heavy users online; New York's 75% wholesale tax adds about USD 2 to a can.
  • The US Food and Drug Administration has authorised 39 new pouch products since May 2026, plus 24 for British American Tobacco's Velo brand.
  • Manufacturers are fighting for share (Velo rose from about 16% to about 30% of United States volume in a year), and every product launch makes the manufacturer a buyer of visibility on Haypp's websites.

Inference: two external drivers work on two different lines of the income statement. Channel migration drives customers and revenue. Migration is slow, compounding and largely beyond anyone's power to accelerate, which is why much of Haypp's paid marketing in 2026 bought customers who would have come anyway. Manufacturers' rivalry drives supplier-paid income and therefore profit. Rivalry acts faster, is set once a year by contract, and is currently rising into 2027.

The headwinds: few are gradual, and several are sudden.

  1. Reported growth overstates the structural rate. Reported 2026 growth of about 25% compares against a United States business that lacked ZYN until 11 September 2025, and Core's growth includes a new Swedish excise duty and manufacturer price rises passed through to customers. From the fourth quarter of 2026 the comparison is clean, and we expect group growth to drop from 28% to about 19% in one step.
  2. ZYN's larger can. ZYN's move from 15 to 20 pouches a can cuts revenue per pouch by about 25% until late 2027. On the earlier Analyst's estimate, the larger can takes about 2% off group revenue and almost nothing off profit.
  3. Regulation cuts both ways. The United Kingdom's advertising ban from 1 June 2027 hurts rivals that depend on paid marketing more than it hurts Haypp. Against that, eight EU states want a ban on cross-border online sales (the European Commission's proposal is due around the turn of the year), a Swedish court now requires biometric checks at parcel lockers, and United States cities have fined Haypp twice in a year.
  4. Markets and currency. The market regime is hostile to small, illiquid growth shares, and about half of Haypp's revenue is in unhedged foreign currency.

So what. The environment supports 13% to 16% revenue growth for years, with low cyclicality: demand is habitual, returning customers provide over 90% of sales, and tighter household budgets send users to the cheaper online channel. The environment gives much weaker support to the level of profit in any one year.

Strongest counter-case. The same three manufacturers that fund Haypp's profit can withdraw their products, and as online grows they have reasons to want the customer relationship for themselves. A calmer or more consolidated manufacturer field would cut the media budgets on which Haypp's profit depends. Daily pouch use in the United States may also plateau below the online threshold for most users, capping online penetration well short of Nordic levels.

What would change my view. Upward: evidence that United States online penetration is rising faster than users' consumption alone implies, such as Growth adding more than 20,000 active customers a quarter without paid marketing. Downward: a manufacturer restricting online supply or terms; a large state banning flavours or restricting delivery; or a European Commission draft that includes a cross-border online ban with a near date.

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the published narrative (in substance, Deutsche Bank's) on the direction and durability of channel migration. I differ on two points. First, the narrative omits the size of the coming growth slowdown: the two brokers imply fourth-quarter growth of about 23%, and a step down to about 19% is likely to be read first as weaker demand, when it is arithmetic. Second, I am more positive than the cautious view on the near-term supplier backdrop. The evidence for 2027 points to rising manufacturer spending, and the research could not confirm the bear case that trade budgets are about to be cut.

Score: 74, set by the Rater. A structural, multi-year channel migration (online about 3% of US and 7% of UK pouch sales against 36% in Sweden, users crossing the 7-8 pouches-a-day threshold), a category growing about 21% a year, state taxes pushing heavy users online and manufacturer rivalry buying visibility support 13-16% revenue growth for years with low cyclicality; consensus sales growth at the 96th percentile is flattered by the ZYN base effect, and the forces are trimmed by direct threats to them (supplier control of supply, a possible EU cross-border ban, US fines, the larger ZYN can) and give weaker support to profit. Close to the External change forces group's 72: a strong, visible leg reaching most of revenue but trimmed, so just below Helios Towers.

2Internally driven corporate change forces

Bottom line: the internal change is one lever, cost restraint on a finished build-out. Cost restraint is well resourced and plausible, but so far it rests on one admission by management and one flat quarter of overheads.

Evidence: the strategy is unchanged; its intensity changed twice in eighteen months. The strategy is to repeat the Nordic online model in the United States and the United Kingdom, funded by Core. The first change was an acceleration. Marketing rose from 1.0% of sales in the third quarter of 2025 to 3.2% a year later, and headcount rose from 261 to 304 as Haypp added regional presidents, United States legal and regulatory staff, and central teams. The second change was a reversal. At the third-quarter 2026 report, management said its own analysis showed that many customers bought through paid lower-funnel channels would have arrived without payment, and that marketing spending would be reduced and redirected to price and product from the fourth quarter.

Several projects around this reversal are complete. The systems migration finished on 8 December 2025. Haypp runs four automated warehouses, with the Texas warehouse at about a third of capacity. The perimeter is tidier: the United Kingdom vape business, Austria and a small Swedish site have closed, and Saudi Arabia has opened as a cheap option costing about SEK 4m a quarter.

Inference: the internal change force is real but narrow. Haypp has no new management, no new capital-allocation lever, no acquisition programme and no price initiative. One change matters: a cost base built for a much larger business has stopped growing, or management says it has. The whole profit forecast is therefore a forecast of management's spending behaviour (judgement 2). Management showed cost restraint in 2024, when supply and regulation constrained it, and did not show restraint in 2026, when those constraints lifted. In the first half of 2027 the constraints are still lifted, and the United Kingdom advertising window closes on 1 June 2027, which gives management a reason to spend before it closes.

Key messageThe profit forecast is a forecast of cost behaviour: gross profit keeps growing by SEK 170m to 200m a year, and costs must grow by only SEK 78m in 2027, after SEK 211m in 2026.
For restraint

What supports restraint this time. (a) The finding that paid marketing bought few extra customers makes restraint rational, not forced: more paid spending does not buy more growth. (b) Overheads were flat between the second and third quarters of 2026. (c) Executives have co-invested in an incentive plan whose shares convert only above 130% of the issue price. The plan targets 2028, the year of a margin target whose low end is the one target wholly within management's control. (d) From June 2027 the law removes the main paid marketing channels in the United Kingdom.

Against restraint

What weakens the case for restraint. One flat quarter is thin evidence. Supplier-paid income growing by about SEK 170m a year is unlikely to need no extra analysts, studies or consumer panels, and those costs sit in overhead. Two fines argue for more compliance spending. New markets incur costs before they earn revenue.

So what. The marketing reallocation matters less for 2027 than the headlines suggest. Our 2027 marketing assumption of 2.2% of sales is level with the 2026 average of 2.25%; the 3.2% was an exit rate, not the year's average. The margin recovery comes from overheads growing 8% to 9% while revenue grows 16%.

Strongest counter-case. Management is a growth-first team, led by a chief executive who wants "as much flexibility as possible to land grab". If Growth customer additions slow after the marketing cut, management's likeliest response is to spend again. Management's record supports this reading (topic 4).

What would change my view. Upward: two consecutive quarters with marketing at or below 2.4% of sales, overheads at or below SEK 140m a quarter, and Growth still adding 13,000 or more active customers a quarter. Downward: marketing back above 2.8% of sales, or management's phrase "investment elevated through mid-2027" becoming "through 2027" on the February call.

Where I differ from the market. Deutsche Bank reads the marketing cut as easing the drag on margins. I read the cut as restoring a normal run-rate. No published research frames the margin recovery as a question of cost behaviour, which is where I think the debate belongs.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The internal force is one lever: cost restraint on a finished build-out (systems migration, four automated warehouses, perimeter tidied) after marketing rose from 1.0% to 3.2% of sales and was found largely wasteful; if held it drives most of the forecast 2027 EBITDA gain, but it is evidenced by one admission and one flat quarter, against a 2026 overspend, recurring items and compliance costs. I sit a little above the Internal change forces group's 50 because the build-out is funded and complete and the restraint is rational rather than forced, but it is gently positive and unproven, below Shell's evidenced self-help-plus.

3Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Bottom line: Haypp's industry position and customer franchise are well above average, its financial profile and earnings quality are below average today, and its management is a capable builder whose financial promises need discounting. The result is a medium-quality, non-cyclical business with a high-quality core.

Industry structure: four forces are favourable and one is hostile, and the hostile force is the strongest. Among online retailers Haypp has no serious rival: Haypp is about 14 times the size of the next largest, roughly 60 challengers have failed, and manufacturers' own websites hold about 1% of online volume. Customers are fragmented and loyal to the platform. The substitute, the physical store, is losing its heaviest users. Compliance costs that rise with every new rule deter new entrants. The hostile force is supplier power. Mutual interest holds supplier power in check: manufacturers earn about 15% more selling through Haypp than through stores, use Haypp to launch and test products, and buy its data.

The moat is distribution and data, not price or product. Haypp has four real advantages: customer acquisition without payment (about 97% of traffic is unpaid); scale in buying and fulfilment, deliberately given back to customers as lower prices; its data and advertising position with manufacturers; and compliance capability (Haypp deployed biometric locker checks within weeks of the Swedish court ruling). Haypp has no pricing power over consumers and wants none; its prices follow manufacturers' list prices and taxes.

Two derived findings change how the moat should be read.

  • Core's record margin is supplier income. Subtracting orders times average order value from segment revenue leaves about SEK 106m of supplier-paid income in Core in the third quarter of 2026 (up about 49%) and about SEK 42m in Growth (up about 26%). Core's whole EBITDA of SEK 104m roughly equals its supplier income. Without supplier income, the group's retail operation would lose roughly SEK 90m a quarter. Core is therefore not a separate, safer engine; it shares the group's dependence on suppliers. One point mitigates that dependence: Nordic supplier income rests on advertising restrictions as well as on rivalry. Where display and product descriptions are banned, Haypp's website is one of the few lawful places a manufacturer can present a product.
  • The Growth customer is already worth about as much as the Core customer. Revenue per active customer in the third quarter was SEK 1,713 in Growth and SEK 1,829 in Core, because Haypp's American customers are heavy users paying American prices. Growth loses money because a third of the group's customers carry about 59% of its overhead, not because the Growth customer is worth less. Growth's breakeven is then arithmetic: at a contribution of about 12% of revenue, an overhead of about SEK 330m needs revenue of about SEK 2.8bn, which our forecast reaches in 2028 to 2029. No published research makes this positive point.

Financial profile: a sound engine with thin, managed and noisy earnings. The strengths are an asset-light model, low working capital, net cash excluding leases, and a Core segment that proves the economics of a mature market. The weaknesses matter more for valuation than for the business:

  • Thin margins. The adjusted EBIT margin was 2.5%, 3.7% and 3.9% in 2023 to 2025 and is about 2.3% in 2026. The gross margin rose from 12.7% to 19.7% over the same period, but part of that rise came from United States warehouse costs moving from cost of goods to depreciation when the Texas warehouse was automated. Progress is therefore better judged on EBIT than on gross margin or EBITDA.
  • Low earnings quality. Reported EPS has been under 42% of the brokers' adjusted EPS in every year from 2023 to 2025, and is negative in 2026. Items affecting comparability have recurred every year (SEK 30m, SEK 53m and about SEK 65m). They include United States legal costs three years running, and cash bonuses that fund executives' purchases of shares in the incentive plan. Treating those items as the operating costs they have proved to be lowers 2027 EPS by about 17%.
  • Weak cash conversion. Free cash flow after capitalised software and leases was SEK 63m in 2024 and SEK 22m in 2025 on Deutsche Bank's count, a fraction of adjusted earnings.

Management: trust the direction and the operations, but discount the timing of financial promises. Gavin O'Dowd (chief executive since 2017, formerly of British American Tobacco) built the category leader, won ZYN back through a deal structured around supplier services, and delivered the technology and warehouse programme on time. He owns just under 3% of the company. Against that record, the listing-era target of SEK 5bn of sales in 2025 was missed by 23% and re-dated; paid marketing was praised and then found largely wasteful; and management withholds the two numbers that most affect EPS (the marketing plan and the nature of the legal items). Governance is adequate, not prudent: a paid consultant sits on the board, and the audit committee is the whole board. The culture has the low-cost, share-the-savings logic of the best operators, but not yet their discipline in cost, compliance or communication.

So what. Haypp's foundations justify confidence that it will dominate a growing channel. They do not justify confidence in any particular year's EPS, and they explain why: profit is a residual that management sets, paid for by counterparties two orders of magnitude larger than Haypp.

Strongest counter-case. "A flywheel is not a moat." Haypp's data is valuable only while manufacturers lack equivalent direct data, and the more manufacturers pay for access to Haypp's customers, the stronger their reason to own those customers. AI-mediated search could also weaken Haypp's advantage in unpaid traffic; there is no evidence either way yet.

What would change my view. Upward: a multi-year supply and media agreement with a major manufacturer, or a first year in which reported and adjusted earnings converge. Downward: a manufacturer launching a multi-brand or marketplace route to the heavy user, or a rising paid share of new customers without faster customer growth.

Where I differ from the market. Deutsche Bank treats supplier-paid income as an under-appreciated barrier to entry. I agree that supplier-paid income is the moat, and add that it is also the dependency, in Core as much as in Growth. I am more positive than the earlier Analyst and the market on the value of the United States customer, and therefore on where the Growth margin can settle once scale covers overhead.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Qualitatively above average: about 14 times the next online rival, about 97% unpaid traffic, data and media sold to manufacturers, compliance as a barrier and habitual, non-cyclical demand (Industry 70, Competitive advantage 66); but the hostile force is the strongest one, three suppliers holding about 87% of volume, there is no consumer pricing power, and the Growth build-out has so far earned a negative return. The financial profile is weak (return on invested capital 5.9%, 44th percentile; operating margin at the 9th; reported EPS under 42% of adjusted; thin free cash flow; Economic strength 33) and management misses its financial promises (Management 45), so predictability pulls a high-quality core down to a medium-quality whole, level with Shell and below Helios Towers' proven unit economics.

4Guidance: conservatism, proactivity and track record

Bottom line: Haypp's guidance is neither conservative nor managed down, and its record is of revenue delivered and profit missed, so this element of your framework is absent today.

Evidence: the only formal guidance is a 2028 target, and our forecast misses two of its three parts. Haypp gives no annual guidance. The 2028 target, set in April 2025, has three parts: revenue growing 18% to 25% a year at constant currency from 2024 (a floor of about SEK 7.1bn, or about SEK 6.95bn in today's kronor); an adjusted EBIT margin of 5.5% plus or minus 1.5 points; and an ambition of three to four times 2024's adjusted EBIT (SEK 404m to 538m). Our 2028 forecast is revenue of SEK 6.34bn, a margin of 4.8% and adjusted EBIT of SEK 303m. Our revenue is short of the floor, our margin is inside the range at its low end, and our EBIT is short of the ambition. Deutsche Bank's revenue forecast sits exactly on the floor, and no published forecast reaches the EBIT ambition.

The record: targets are never raised and never cut in advance; they are re-dated late. Group profit has fallen short of the broker benchmark in at least four of the last six quarters, by 12% to 24%, each time because of costs that management chose to incur. Revenue, by contrast, has met or slightly beaten the benchmark, except when a supplier removed a brand. Haypp compiles and publishes its own pre-results consensus, and that consensus defines each beat or miss.

Inference: on each of this topic's three tests, the answer is negative. Haypp's guidance is not conservative: because 2025 was a lost year, even the revenue floor now needs about 21% growth a year in 2027 and 2028. Management does not keep expectations low; its informal tone ("comfortably on track", growth described as "exponential") runs ahead of the brokers. And Haypp has no record of raising guidance, or of estimates rising behind delivery.

So what, constructively. Without annual guidance there is little to cut before 2028, and because even the most bullish broker sits only at the revenue floor, the market already partly expects Haypp to miss its targets. The earlier Analyst puts the chance that the revenue target is re-dated, replaced or qualified by May 2028 at about 40%, most likely at the fourth-quarter 2027 report or at a capital markets day. A re-dating need not read badly: 2030 targets on the scale Deutsche Bank already models (about SEK 10bn of revenue) would look like progress. The guidance that can move estimates inside six months is informal: what management says on 10 February 2027 about spending in the first half.

Strongest counter-case. The margin range is the one target management fully controls, the incentive plan points at 2028, and a team that has just admitted over-spending may over-correct. If so, profit delivery could turn before the record suggests.

What would change my view. A first quarter in which adjusted EBIT beats the company-compiled consensus because of costs rather than gross margin, or any quantified statement of the 2027 marketing budget.

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the market's implicit view that the 2028 targets are an ambition, not a commitment. I differ from the median broker in not adopting the revenue floor as a forecast.

Score: 25, set by the Rater. No annual guidance (neutral in itself), but the listing-era SEK 5bn 2025 sales target was missed by 23% and re-dated, the 2028 target is not conservative (even the revenue floor needs about 21% a year and no forecast reaches the EBIT ambition, a re-dating about 40% likely), group profit missed the broker benchmark in at least four of the last six quarters by 12-24% on costs management chose, and the informal tone runs ahead of brokers; revenue delivery is the one redeeming record. Coherent with the Guidance (27) and Sell-side (30) groups: the targets-re-dated pattern of the 25 level, above TT Electronics' restatements and chronic margin misses.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, cost control and feedback loops

Bottom line: Haypp's model has strong latent operating leverage, pricing power on the supplier side and a deep cost cushion, but no consumer pricing power or financial leverage. Converting growth into outsized profit is possible and forecast, but not yet demonstrated.

Evidence: the operating leverage is large and so far unharvested. Variable costs above gross profit are only about 2% of sales, so an extra krona of revenue contributes 16 to 18 öre before marketing, about four times the EBITDA margin. That is high operating leverage by definition. What management has done with that leverage is the central exhibit of this memo:

SEK m202420252026E2027E2028E
Gross profit added in the year+150+175+194+167+179
Costs added between gross profit and EBITDA+45+148+211+78+57
EBITDA added+105+27-17+89+122
Share of extra gross profit kept70%15%none53%68%

The forecast asks nothing new of gross profit. It asks cost growth to fall by almost two-thirds and stay there. Over 2023 to 2026, each extra krona of revenue produced 7 öre of EBITDA; the forecast needs 12 öre in 2027 and 13 to 15 öre after that. The path has a precedent: Chewy's EBITDA margin rose from 3.3% to about 5.6% in two years on overhead absorption and sponsored advertising, close to what the forecast asks of Haypp between 2026 and 2028.

Inference 1: the "price" in this business is charged to suppliers, and two very different transmission rates follow. A krona of product revenue leaves 6 to 7 öre of profit; a krona of supplier-paid income leaves nearly all of it. The events that move revenue most (the base effect, the larger ZYN can, promotions, currency) therefore move profit least. The events that move profit most are upstream: how many manufacturers are fighting for share, how many products they are launching, and how many other advertising routes the law has closed. This distinction matters practically for the next four quarters. Weak reported revenue with supplier income and costs on track would be a false alarm. Revenue on track with supplier income flat as a share of sales would be a false comfort.

Inference 2: a real cost cushion converts profit risk into growth risk. Management could cut marketing to about 1% of sales, pause Saudi Arabia and trim price reinvestment. Together those steps are worth about SEK 110m to 130m, two-thirds of 2027 adjusted EBIT, and are available within two or three quarters. Haypp also holds a latent consumer price lever: each point of price in Growth is worth about SEK 20m to 26m, against an online discount of 40% to 50% to stores. Management has shown no wish to use that lever.

Inference 3: the same management behaviour cuts off both tails of profit, and the upper tail more. If revenue falls short, management cuts costs and profit is partly protected. If revenue runs ahead, management treats the window as open and spends the gain. Revenue growth has therefore not yet led to outsized profit growth: the business model allows it, and management's choices have so far prevented it.

Other elements. Financial leverage is nil: net debt of SEK 96m consists of leases, there are no buybacks, and all EPS growth must come from operations. Haypp has five reinforcing loops: buying scale and price; data and media; unpaid search traffic; the usage threshold; and the regulatory sieve that removes weaker rivals. Four of those loops widen volume and share, because their gains are given back in price. The loop that widens margin is fixed-cost absorption. One natural hedge is under-appreciated: fierce manufacturer rivalry lifts supplier income but depresses Growth's price and mix, and calmer rivalry does the reverse.

Strongest counter-case. "Scale economies shared" is Haypp's stated model, so the operating margin is thin by design and may stay thin: every gain is a candidate for reinvestment. On that reading, the low end of the 2028 margin target is a ceiling, not a floor.

What would change my view. The share of extra gross profit kept as EBITDA is the single ratio to watch. A share above 50% for the four quarters to September 2027 would confirm the model; a share below 30% would say that 2026 was the norm.

Where I differ from the market. The brokers model operating leverage as arriving because the build-out is finished. I think the leverage arrives only if management chooses to keep it, and I would weight the table above more heavily than the finished build-out.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. The structure has large operating leverage (variable costs above gross profit only about 2% of sales, so an extra krona contributes 16-18 öre against a 4-6% EBITDA margin), supplier-side pricing power (supplier-paid income carries almost no direct cost), fixed-cost absorption on a platform built for twice the volume and a SEK 110-130m cost cushion; but there is no consumer pricing power or financial leverage, and the gearing has not been harvested (15% of extra gross profit kept in 2025, none in 2026), the case Richard warns of, so the forecast EPS-to-revenue ratio of about 3.5 times is promised rather than proven. Between the 75 level (two gears, one missing) and the 50, and above the Economic strength group's 33 because this topic judges structure, not today's margin.

Does the forecast meet this topic's tests? Yes on growth, and yes on margins against the past, with a caveat on timing.

  • Growth. Revenue grows at double digits every year. EPS compounds at about 56% a year from the 2026 trough, and at about 32% a year from 2025.
  • Margins. The EBITDA margin passes its previous peak in 2028, and the 2028 adjusted EBIT margin of 4.8% passes the 2025 peak by about a point. Growth is forecast to break even during 2028 and to reach a 4% EBITDA margin by 2030.
  • Timing and concentration. About 80% of the increase in adjusted EBIT from 2026 to 2030 arrives in 2028 to 2030. Two-thirds of the EBITDA increase is one item: Growth moving from a loss of SEK 144m to a profit of SEK 162m.

What the numbers rest on.

  • Core: customers up 5% to 6% a year and spend per customer up 2% to 3%, so Core's growth slows from 16% to 8% as the 2026 excise and price rises drop out.
  • Growth: sequential revenue growth of about 7.5% a quarter in 2027, against 7% to 9% in 2026 with heavy marketing. The brokers' split needs about 11% a quarter.
  • Gross margin: up 0.3 points a year.
  • Marketing: 2.2% of sales, falling to 1.8%.
  • Overheads: growing 7% to 8% a year, which supplies 2.3 of the 3.8 points of margin gain to 2030.

The gap to the brokers is smaller in substance than in the headline. For 2027, our EBITDA is level with Pareto's and 13% below Deutsche Bank's. Of the EPS gap to the brokers' median (SEK 5.80 against our SEK 4.26), about two-thirds is operations (SEK 45m of EBITDA) and about one-third is accounting convention. Deutsche Bank uses a normalised tax rate of 20.6%, where we use 25% because the United States and United Kingdom companies lose money without tax relief, and Deutsche Bank assumes slightly lower depreciation. A quarter's results can settle only the operational part of the gap. For 2028 we are below all three brokers, because of Growth revenue.

Cash lags profit, but a net cash pile builds. The model shows equity free cash flow of SEK 92m in 2027 and SEK 184m in 2028. The model has no line for the cash cost of items affecting comparability, so I would use about SEK 45m to 50m for 2027 (about 1% of market value) and about SEK 160m for 2028. For the same reason, and because of a phasing artefact in the fourth quarter of 2026, I would not quote the model's net cash line. Net cash of roughly SEK 0.7bn by 2030 (about 14% of today's market value) is the better figure, and it is a capital-return option that nobody models and the company has not mentioned.

Strongest counter-case. Upward: the gross-margin input implies the product margin falling from 8.4% to 7.3% in 2027, when the product margin was flat in the latest quarter. If the product margin holds and supplier income grows 30%, 2027 EBITDA is nearer SEK 360m, which is Deutsche Bank's figure. Downward: the 2029 and 2030 margins are the least evidenced part of the forecast, and they are the part on which the 18-month return depends.

What would change my view. I would move 2028 revenue towards the brokers' figures if Growth holds sequential growth above 9% a quarter through the first half of 2027 with marketing at or below 2.4% of sales.

Where I differ from the market. On direction, not at all. On size and timing, I put 2027 at Pareto's level operationally and 2028 below every broker on Growth revenue.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Above 35% gives C because very high growth from the 2026 trough is hard to predict; on the cleaner 2025 base (about 3.3) the rate would be about 32%, a B, so I place it high in the C band: the growth is wholly organic, revenue compounds at about 16% and the margin path rises above anything in the record from 2028, held below the top of the band because it is back-end loaded (about 80% of the EBIT gain in 2028-30) and concentrated in Growth turning profitable.

Estimates: cuts are more likely than upgrades to come first. The first test falls on revenue, the one line with a clean delivery record. The two brokers' full-year revenue forecasts imply fourth-quarter revenue of about SEK 1,295m (+23%); ours is SEK 1,248m. Their implied fourth-quarter EBITDA equals ours. If we are right, the February report shows revenue about 4% below the brokers' figure with profit in line, the reverse of the past year's pattern. I hold this view with only moderate confidence: most of the revenue difference is in Core, and it rests on an inference that the year-earlier quarter was swollen by buying ahead of the excise increase. The earlier Analyst puts the chance that the 2027 median EPS is lower after February at about 55%, and lower by 10% to 20% by August at about 70%; I have no reason to differ. Haypp will almost certainly repeat its guidance unchanged at each 2027 report.

Where upgrades could come from.

  1. The 2027 supplier contracts (judgement 3), visible in the May report.
  2. Core, which beat Deutsche Bank's estimate by 15% in the third quarter, and which Deutsche Bank models at a 2027 margin below the latest quarter's.
  3. A base effect in our favour from late 2027. If estimates have come down to about our level and Haypp delivers the margin step, the same results that would disappoint against EPS of SEK 5.80 would beat against SEK 4.3.

Upgrades in the full sense, meaning rising 2028 estimates, need Growth revenue up about 40% with costs held.

The narrative already contains the favourable points; what it omits is cautious near term and positive further out. The published narrative is one bullish broker's, and it already contains the migration, the Growth margin path, regulation as a barrier to entry and supplier income as a flywheel. What the narrative does not contain is mostly cautious for the next six to twelve months: the size of the growth slowdown, the dependence on cost behaviour, the earnings conventions, and the multiple on lower estimates. Further out, what it omits is positive: the value of the American customer, the re-pricing of supplier contracts, the tax shelter once Growth is profitable, and the cash pile. Novel positive news inside twelve months is scarce and dated: the May supplier-income reading, the United Kingdom advertising ban consolidating that market from June, and the August margin step. A capital markets day with 2030 targets is about an even chance within 18 months, and would be the natural moment for the narrative to move on.

So what. The scope for upgrades in the next six months is low. From the second half of 2027 it improves materially, and more so if estimates fall first. For an investor who wants positively skewed revisions, the timing of entry matters more here than the view of the business.

Strongest counter-case. Fourth-quarter revenue lands at the brokers' level, supplier income steps up in Growth, and estimates never come down. That is the upper case, and it would make today's price the cheapest entry of the next year.

What would change my view. Fourth-quarter revenue at or above SEK 1,290m, with Growth active customers at 240,000 or more, would move me towards the brokers before the margin evidence arrives.

Where I differ from the market. The brokers' 2027 path requires upgrades to our forecast; I think the brokers' forecasts are more likely to come down to ours.

8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Bottom line: momentum is weak on earnings revisions, neutral on price, absent on guidance and unhelpful among peers. The one strong element, rising target prices, is as much a warning as a support.

Evidence (dashboard, 11 November 2026).

  • Guidance: nothing to upgrade; the 2028 targets are repeated.
  • Sell-side earnings momentum, grade D. The mean 2027 EPS estimate is down 7% over one month, 5% over three months, 20% over six months and 47% over twelve months. EBITDA estimates are down 32% over twelve months but up 6% over three months. Revenue estimates have moved 1% in a year. Target prices are up 7%, 21% and 25% over one, three and six months.
  • Technical momentum, grade C. The share price is 13% above its 200-day average, which has risen in six of the last twelve months. Returns are +5%, +8% and +9% over three, six and twelve months, and relative strength is at the 60th percentile of the universe.
  • Valuation, grade F. The current P/E is at the 87th percentile of its own history.

Inference: the components of momentum contradict one another in an informative way. Target prices are rising while earnings estimates fall, because the brokers have moved their valuation anchor from 2027 to 2028 and beyond. The shares have therefore re-rated on a year that has barely been tested. The share price is holding up on a rising multiple, not on rising earnings.

Two readings of the revision data matter. First, the revision statistics overstate how far estimates have been reset. With three contributors, the mean mostly records which brokers are included: DNB Carnegie left in June with a high estimate, and Pareto arrived with a low one. Deutsche Bank, the broker that sets the median, has a higher 2027 EPS today (SEK 5.80) than in April (SEK 5.26). The fall of 47% therefore does not mean the reset is done; at the median, 2027 and 2028 estimates are untouched. Second, Haypp's peers offer no lead. Over the latest six months, the basket of tobacco peers explained about 1% of the variance of Haypp's daily returns, so there is no sector tide to carry Haypp's shares or to catch them.

So what. Nothing in present momentum argues for urgency. The combination your framework looks for (rising guidance, rising estimates, a strengthening narrative and price confirmation) is absent on the first two counts, present in a single broker's voice on the third, and lukewarm on the fourth.

Strongest counter-case. The three-month rise in EBITDA estimates and a share price above every moving average are how turns begin, and with thin coverage a single upgrade moves the statistics a long way.

What would change my view. Deutsche Bank and Pareto both raising 2027 EBITDA after a report, or the dashboard's earnings-momentum grade moving to C or better on a rising median rather than on a change of contributors.

Where I differ from the market. The market reads rising target prices as confirmation. I read them as the valuation running ahead of estimates that have not yet been tested.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. Both measures positive would give B, but the parts strongly contradict them, so I move it one step to C: guidance absent, mean 2027 EPS down 7%, 20% and 47% over one, six and twelve months (six-month revision at the 11th percentile), only a third of analysts at Buy (27th percentile), and the memo grading earnings momentum D. Placed in the upper half of C because the price is 13% above a rising 200-day average, three-month EBITDA estimates are up 6% and target prices up 25% in six months; peers give no lead.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Bottom line: the case is simple, non-cyclical and unusually trackable, but its earnings are fragile to small errors, and its tails are sudden, correlated and large for the share price. It is a higher-risk case than its staple-like demand suggests.

Simple in structure. Three reported quantities decide the case, and five published figures rebuild the income statement down to adjusted EBITDA each quarter. Few companies of Haypp's size can be rebuilt line by line from their own reports. The business is narrow: one category, one channel, two segments. Demand is staple-like and, if anything, counter-cyclical.

Fragile in numbers, for five reasons that compound.

  1. A thin margin. Haypp's quarterly profit shortfalls over the past year were SEK 4m to 9m: only 0.3 to 0.8 points of margin, but 12% to 24% of profit. The same error against 2028's profit would be 5% to 12%. Predictability therefore improves with every point of margin gained and worsens with every point lost, a reinforcing loop in the share's risk as well as in its earnings.
  2. One behaviour: management's cost restraint (judgement 2).
  3. One income stream and three payers (judgement 3). On the earlier Analyst's driver table, about 94% of the forecast growth in gross profit to 2030 is supplier-paid.
  4. Four items between EBIT and EPS that nobody can forecast: items affecting comparability, acquisition amortisation, currency revaluation in finance costs, and tax (whose rate has run at 36%, 24%, 7.5% and then negative). As a result, 2027 has three EPS figures, shown below. Valuation, ours and the brokers', uses the highest.
  5. A valuation with no anchor beneath it (topics 11 and 12).

The range of 2027 outcomes is symmetric for revenue but skewed down for EPS. Revenue ranges from SEK 5.2bn to 5.85bn, about 6% either way of our base. EBITDA ranges from about SEK 245m to 370m. EPS ranges from about -45% to +35% around our base. The EPS range is skewed down for the reasons in topic 5, and because the negative tails are sudden while their positive counterpart (United States online penetration doubling) works over years.

Sudden, high-impact risks, ranked by expected damage. The probabilities are the earlier Analyst's judgements over 18 months, which I accept.

These risks are correlated: regulatory pressure prompted the 2024 supply pause. Combined, the chance of at least one material event is perhaps 15% to 25%, of which about 12% would land on 2027 earnings.

Sector and industry precedents: concentrated payers are the failure mode. Across retail media and nicotine distribution, the pattern is consistent. Criteo's retail-media revenue fell about 20% when its largest client took the work in-house; Scandinavian Tobacco lost the zyn.com contract and 10% of its North American online sales; and Instacart missed on advertising when a few large advertisers cut spending. Among online specialists in investment phases, those that re-rated had visible margin protection or accelerating growth, and those that de-rated had slowing growth or debt. Haypp shares the first group's growth and balance sheet, but has not yet shown its margin protection.

How far the shares could fall, and how often they have. Haypp's two-year-forward multiple has ranged from about 7 times (mid-2022) to about 20 times, and fell to about 9 to 10 times in the licence and ZYN panic of late 2024. The share price has fallen by about a third or more twice in the past 27 months (from about SEK 110 to SEK 60 between August and December 2024, and from SEK 164 to SEK 114 between September 2025 and January 2026), and each time recovered most of the fall within about five months. At a trough multiple of 10 to 12 times today's forward estimates, the shares would be at SEK 80 to 95; with estimates 25% lower, at SEK 60 to 70. Illiquidity (about USD 0.5m traded a day), exclusion from many Nordic funds, and coverage by only three brokers amplify moves in both directions. Below about 10 times, Core alone would be valued at little more than a manufacturer's multiple, the level at which interest from private-equity buyers becomes plausible.

Trackability, the can-do part: the risks to the base case are unusually easy to watch. Five published indicators, listed in order of reliability for the next two reports, show on each results day whether the base case holds:

What would change my view. A lower risk assessment needs margin, not narrative: each point of group margin gained roughly halves the percentage damage of a given forecast error.

Where I differ from the market. The published view treats supplier power as "muted" and attaches no probability to it. I think supplier power deserves a probability, and that probability is not small.

That is the 25 level's range of a third or more; coherent with the Risks groups (25 and 38), lifted just above Entra by the trackability and net cash.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Bottom line: the stock is turning up but unconfirmed until at least mid-August 2027, while expectations and the multiple already sit where a broadening thesis would put them.

My assessment: turning up, unconfirmed, and priced as if the thesis were already broadening. The dashboard's rule gives the same starting phase (Turning/Inflecting), and I agree with it.

The evidence for "turning up". The revenue cycle turned a year ago. The margin trough is the second half of 2026. Core's margin has already turned to a record. The cause of the trough was largely self-inflicted and is being corrected. The cost base has stopped growing for one quarter.

The evidence for "unconfirmed". No quarter has yet shown group margin rising year on year, and the next two quarters cannot. The median broker has not reset its estimates. Profit delivery against expectations has not turned.

The evidence for "priced as broadening". The multiple is in the top fifth of its history on the brokers' numbers, and above its 90th percentile on ours. Target prices have risen 25% in six months.

So what. In your terms, the fundamentals are at an early phase and the valuation at a late one. That mismatch is the main risk to the shares over the next six months, and it is why the next phase could come by either of two paths. The first path is forward, into thesis broadening, if the August and November 2027 reports deliver. The second path is back through a de-rating first, if the February and May reports disappoint against the brokers while the business stays on our track. The second path would not mean the business had stalled; it would mean the share price catching down to the business's phase.

Strongest counter-case. The business is further along than I credit. Core's record margin, Growth customers up 55% and a completed platform are thesis-broadening facts, and the market is right to pay for them ahead of the group margin.

What would change my view. I would move the phase to thesis broadening on two consecutive quarters of year-on-year group margin gain with Growth customers still compounding, which cannot happen before November 2027, or earlier on a clear step-up in supplier income under the 2027 contracts. I would move the phase to stalling if Growth customers stop growing after the marketing cut, or if marketing returns above 2.8% of sales.

Where I differ from the market. The market is treating the turn as done. I treat the turn as probable but unproven.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's turning up, unconfirmed (over the computed Reinforcing): the revenue cycle and Core margin have turned and the trough cause is being corrected, but no quarter has shown group margin up year on year, the next two reports can only disappoint, the median broker has not reset and the multiple already sits in the top fifth of its history. Early fundamentals with late-phase pricing make the next six months a likely price catch-down before any broadening, so below Solid State's plausible Bottoming-to-Turning and just above Linea Directa's turnaround not yet in forecasts.

11The fair multiple

Bottom line: the guideline of 14.45 times is a reasonable and slightly conservative fair multiple for an unconfirmed turn. A case for about 16 to 17 times can be made only once the margin recovery is demonstrated.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline for the Turning/Inflecting phase is 14.45 times two-year-forward earnings, the 60th percentile of the stock's own history (59 months, back to the 2021 listing). The guideline lies between the ten-year median of 13.3 times and the 75th percentile of 16.6 times. The shares trade on 18.4 times the brokers' two-year-forward EPS and on 23.9 times ours.

My view: 14.45 times is a fair central figure for today's phase, and if anything slightly conservative when applied to our earnings. I would use a range of about 13 to 17 times, and stay in the lower half of that range until the August 2027 evidence arrives.

Arguments for a higher multiple.

  • The historical multiple was struck on forecasts that did not arrive. In late 2024 the shares traded on about 10 times two-year-forward estimates, but the year those estimates referred to, 2026, is coming in at roughly a third of what the brokers then expected. Investors who thought they paid 10 times paid nearer 28 times delivered earnings. A percentile of that history, applied to a forecast we have deliberately leaned down, is therefore a stricter test than the market has applied to itself.
  • The phase may be different at the horizon. The guideline is for a turning phase. If the base case delivers, by spring 2028 the stock would be in a delivery phase, for which a figure nearer the 75th percentile would be the like-for-like guideline.
  • The fundamentals: a three-to-five-year growth runway, a mature segment that funds it, no debt, and a cash pile building from 2028.

Arguments for a lower multiple.

  • Earnings quality. Adjusted EPS excludes costs that have recurred for three years; including those costs lowers 2027 EPS by about 17% and 2030 EPS by about 4%.
  • Dependence. Profit answers to three suppliers, and the tails are sudden.
  • The holder base. The shares are illiquid, thinly covered and excluded by many funds; exclusion policies are a standing cap on the multiple.
  • No anchor. The manufacturers trade on 6 to 10 times earnings, and Haypp's own panics took its multiple to 8 to 10 times.

So what. The gap between today's multiple and any fair multiple is larger than the debate about the fair multiple itself. Even at 16.6 times, the multiple on our earnings would fall by 31%. The price at which the multiple headwind disappears today is about SEK 94 on our forward earnings and about SEK 116 on the brokers'.

Strongest counter-case. Deutsche Bank's cash-flow valuation supports SEK 220 a share and implies 38 times 2027 earnings, on the argument that a growth-adjusted measure is the right one for a business this early in its margin curve. If Growth reaches Core-like margins, that argument is right, and any percentile of the past five years is too low.

What would change my view. I would argue for the upper half of my range once Growth's loss is narrowing with customers still compounding, and for the lower half if supplier income flattens as a share of sales.

Where I differ from the market. The market is paying a delivery-phase multiple for a turning-phase stock.

Score: 25, set by the Rater. Measure 1 is dear and measure 2 cannot be read (the memo's comparison with manufacturers on 6-10 times is not the stock's cohort and gives no history of its premium), so on measure 1 alone D. Placed at the floor of D because the dearness is only partly deserved: the multiple sits on trough 2026-27 earnings with fast growth ahead, but at 23.9 times the memo's two-year-forward EPS against a fair 14.45 times it prices a delivery phase for a turning-phase stock, and even 16.6 times would mean a 31% de-rating.

12Total shareholder return

Bottom line: at the guideline multiple, the model gives about +1% to March 2028 and +36% to September 2029, all of it from earnings growth set against a 40% fall in the multiple, and none from cash returns. The three-year return is sound; the 18-month return depends on the entry price.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple.

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedValue per shareFrom earningsFrom the multipleFrom dividends
To 31 March 2028 (the 18-month column)+1.1%+0.8%SEK 157+67.4%-39.6%0
To 30 September 2029 (the three-year column)+35.7%+11.2%SEK 210+124.8%-39.6%0

What drives each part.

  • Earnings (+67% and +125%). Two-year-forward EPS rises from SEK 6.48 today (in substance the year to September 2028) to SEK 10.83 at March 2028 and about SEK 14.5 at September 2029. The March 2028 figure rests on 2029 and 2030 earnings (judgement 5). The September 2029 figure covers the year to September 2031, beyond the last year of the forecast inputs, so it contains the model's own extrapolation of about 12% growth in 2031 and should be quoted with that caution.
  • The multiple (-40%). The multiple falls from 23.9 times to 14.45 times, in full by the 18-month column, and is unchanged thereafter. That is why the three-year return is so much better per year than the 18-month return: the de-rating is paid once, and earnings keep compounding.
  • Dividends and other cash returns (nil). Haypp pays no dividend and buys back no shares, and incentive shares dilute holders by about 1% a year. Peers in the sector return 8% to 13% of market value a year; Haypp's whole return must come from operating earnings. Cash returns become possible from about 2029 and are not in the model.

The range around the 18-month figure (value per share at March 2028):

The lower-case and brokers'-path EPS are my estimates: the lower case takes about 30% off our 2029 and 2030 earnings; the brokers' path starts from the one broker's 2029 EPS of SEK 14.00.

Inference: on our forecast, the shares are priced to return nothing for 18 months and a reasonable 11% a year over three years. The centre of the 18-month distribution is near zero, and the range is wide, from about -45% to +55%. The return becomes attractive under any of three conditions: the brokers prove right on earnings; the phase moves on and the fair multiple rises with it; or the price falls first. At SEK 116, for example, the same forecast and multiple give about +35% to March 2028 and about +80% over three years.

Strongest counter-case. The decomposition of return into earnings and multiple assumes the de-rating happens. Shares in a confirmed delivery phase with 40% to 70% EPS growth rarely de-rate to their median, and if the multiple merely holds on our earnings, the 18-month return is the full +67%.

What would change my view. The return case improves one-for-one with evidence that moves 2029 and 2030 earnings. The cleanest such evidence would be Growth's quarterly loss falling below SEK 25m by the third quarter of 2027, from SEK 48m in the latest quarter.

Where I differ from the market. The three brokers' target prices (SEK 160 to 220) imply returns of 3% to 42% over twelve months. On our earnings, those prices in spring 2028 would need a multiple of 15 to 20 times.

Score: 25, set by the Rater. About +1% (67% earnings growth cancelled by a 40% de-rating, no cash returns) sits just inside D, which maps to about 25; the lower tail is fat (lower case -30% at the fair multiple, about a third of the probability on lower or severe cases), which would pull it below nil, but the three-year check of +36% (11% a year) supports holding it at the floor of D rather than F.

13Summary conclusion

The case in one sentenceHaypp is a good business in the making whose investment case today turns on sequence, not quality: the fundamental skew over three to four years is positive, the skew in expectations over the next six to twelve months is negative, and three dated readings in 2027 will show which way the case resolves.

A good business in the making. Haypp has a near-monopoly in a channel that heavy users migrate into mechanically, a mature segment that proves the economics, a finished platform with room for twice the volume, and customers in its growth markets who are already worth as much as those in its home markets. Its earnings are thin, managed and supplier-paid, and its tails are sudden. None of those weaknesses is new, and most of them can be tracked in three published numbers.

The skew splits by horizon. Over three to four years the fundamental skew is positive: EPS is forecast to rise almost sixfold from the 2026 trough, on drivers the business has mostly demonstrated. Over the next six to twelve months the skew in expectations is negative: our forecast is below the brokers on every line, the first test falls in a quarter built to look weak, Haypp has never raised guidance, and the multiple already assumes the turn is complete.

The situation you look for is not here yet, but two dated routes lead to it. Unusually positive skew in both fundamentals and upgrades could arrive through a reset of estimates in February or May followed by delivery from August 2027, or through a step-up in supplier income under the 2027 contracts that pulls our own forecast up. The first route would make the same business a much better proposition, at a lower price or against a lower bar. The second would show that the brokers' bar was right all along.

Memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 72, set by the Rater. A strong, structural external force (topic 1 at 74) is meant to reach profits through one narrow, unproven internal lever (topic 2 at 56), and the financial output is very large (EPS roughly sixfold from the 2026 trough, margins above the record from 2028, consensus EPS growth at the 98th percentile) but from a trough, back-end loaded and not yet visible in any quarter's margin (topic 6 high in C). Clear positive forces with a material effect on forecast profits but with the conversion not yet in results puts it just below the 75 level, in line with the memo's B.

Foundations' Robustness: 50, set by the Rater. A near-monopoly online franchise with habitual, non-cyclical demand, a capital-light model, net cash and a Core segment proving the maturity economics (topic 3 at 55) is offset by profit paid by three far larger suppliers, a 2-3% margin, weak earnings quality, adequate governance and a record of re-dated targets and profit misses (topic 4 at 25). The 50 level's good moats offset by a poor delivery record; unlike CVS Group, the margins are neither stable nor predictable, so stability does not lift it, in line with the memo's C.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 60, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits the Demand-driven EPS step-up setup: the demand step-up (channel migration, Growth customers up about 55%) and the capacity (a platform built for twice the volume) are in place, but the conversion into an EPS step-up rests on cost restraint not yet evidenced and today's problems (the 2026 overspend, profit misses, a thin margin) blur it, so it fits in kind with one important element missing. I sit above the memo's D because its reasons (the step-up below the brokers and already paid for at a top-quintile multiple) are timing and price, which belong to topics 7 and 12.

Case Riskiness: 27, set by the Rater. Topic 9's simple, trackable, non-cyclical, net-cash case does not offset an EPS cone of about -45% to +35%, fragile thin-margin earnings, sudden and correlated supplier and regulatory tails, and a high multiple on an illiquid, thinly covered share with no peer anchor (falls of a third twice in 27 months), so it sits at the 25 level, worse than Arteche's 60 because the earnings themselves are fragile and not only the multiple, in line with the memo's D.

End notes

Conventions. "Our forecast" is the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). Profit and EPS are on the company's adjusted basis (before items affecting comparability and before amortisation of acquired intangibles) unless stated otherwise. "Core" is the Nordic segment; "Growth" is the United States and United Kingdom segment. "Supplier-paid income" is the Media and Insights income that manufacturers pay Haypp for advertising, launch services and consumer data.

Brokers and consensus. Coverage is thin, so this memo does not write "consensus expects". "The two brokers" are Deutsche Bank (Buy, target SEK 220) and Pareto Securities (Hold, SEK 160), the only two that publish revenue and EBITDA on FactSet; Barclays (Overweight, SEK 210) adds a third EPS figure. Consensus estimates are shown by named financial year throughout.

Sources and derived figures. "The earlier Analyst" refers to the earlier analysis sets on Haypp, whose estimates and probabilities this memo cites where stated. "Derived" marks a figure that the earlier Analyst or I calculated from disclosed figures; the company does not publish it. The latest Earnings Review does cover the quarter to 30 September 2026.

2025 figures in the forecast table. The model's own history shows 2025 EBITA of SEK 109m and EPS of SEK 2.99 on FactSet's definition, which is after acquisition amortisation and not comparable with the forecast years. The forecast table therefore shows the company-adjusted 2025 figures instead; the 2025 EPS is the earlier Analyst's estimate.

Forecast inputs. I have not changed any forecast input. The one place where I lean above the inputs (the 2027 gross margin holds a cushion of about SEK 50m) is offset by the one place where I lean below them (cost restraint, worth SEK 30m to 60m if it slips), and neither lean is firm enough to move a line.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
